confirmed.title: Per-account cockpit silently truncates win/loss + revenue-evolution at 100 opportunities, dropping the OLDEST deals
confirmed.evidence: buildCompanyCockpit fetches the account's opportunities with `orderBy: { updatedAt: 'desc' }, take: 100` (queries.ts:237-239), then buildCockpit computes winLoss (cockpit.ts:556-575) and revenueEvolution (cockpit.ts:580-592) by iterating that capped `companyOpps` array in JS. For an enterprise account with >100 opportunities, every closed deal beyond the 100 most-recently-updated is invisible to win-rate, wonValueMicros, lostValueMicros AND the 12-month revenue chart. Worse: because the sort is `updatedAt desc`, the deals that get dropped are the OLDEST — precisely the historical won deals the 'last 12 months close-month rollup' (cockpit.ts:580-592, keyed on dueDate) needs. A large strategic account (the exact target of this cockpit) renders a partial, biased win-rate and a revenue chart missing its earlier months, with no truncation signal to the user. Note accounts.helpers.fetchAccountStats already proves the right pattern (Postgres groupBy, exact regardless of count) and its own doc comment (helpers.ts:28-30) explicitly warns that 'an in-JS reduce over a take-capped findMany silently undercounts pipeline-heavy accounts' — yet the cockpit does exactly that.
confirmed.fix: Derive winLoss counts/sums and the revenue-by-month rollup from Postgres aggregates instead of the take-capped array. Add a groupBy on opportunity stage (and a date_trunc('month', due_date) SUM for revenue) scoped to the account, mirroring fetchAccountStats; keep the take:100 array only for the display lists (open deals, recent activity). At minimum, raise/remove the take for the aggregation inputs and order by dueDate, not updatedAt, so the 12-month window is complete.

verdict.reason:
VERIFIED REAL. The data path is exactly as claimed. dashboard.queries.ts:215-239: buildCompanyCockpit fetches the account's opportunities with `orderBy: { updatedAt: 'desc' }, take: 100`. That capped array is passed straight into buildCockpit as `opportunities` (queries.ts:310), filtered in-memory to `companyOpps` (cockpit.ts:471-474 — a filter that can only shrink the set, never recover dropped rows), and then iterated to compute winLoss (cockpit.ts:556-575: wonCount/lostCount/wonValueMicros/lostValueMicros/winRate) and revenueEvolution (cockpit.ts:580-592: a dueDate-keyed close-month rollup, .slice(-12)). For an account with >100 opportunities, every closed deal beyond the 100 most-recently-updated is invisible to all four numbers, and because the sort is `updatedAt desc` the dropped deals are the least-recently-touched — typically the OLDEST historical won deals, which is precisely what the dueDate-keyed 12-month revenue chart needs for its earlier months. The response (cockpit.ts:594+) carries no truncation flag, so the user sees a complete-looking but biased win-rate and a revenue chart silently missing earlier months.

The reference/contrast in the finding checks out verbatim: accounts.helpers.ts:25-31 documents the correct pattern (Postgres groupBy, 'totals are exact regardless of how many opportunities an account has') and its own warning — 'an in-JS reduce over a take-capped findMany silently undercounts pipeline-heavy accounts' — and fetchAccountStats (helpers.ts:32-90) implements it. The cockpit does exactly what that comment warns against.

Reachability confirmed: GET /crm/companies/:id (routes/crm/companies.ts:155-170) is the live authenticated endpoint backing the single-company cockpit and calls buildCompanyCockpit directly. No Zod/RBAC/query-guard/index mitigates the aggregation defect (the bug is in compute logic, not access). I checked the obvious off-ramps — the companyOpps filter, a hidden pagination/limit guard, and a truncation signal — none rescue it. (Aside, not part of the claim: the cockpit query also omits `deletedAt: null`, unlike fetchAccountStats, so soft-deleted opps are counted too — a separate minor correctness gap.)

SEVERITY ADJUSTED critical -> high. The defect is genuine and clearly wrong for the exact enterprise/strategic-account audience the cockpit targets, but it is a read-only analytics/display panel, not a security, data-loss, multi-tenancy, or outage issue, and it only manifests above 100 opportunities per single account. That is a serious correctness bug (high) rather than critical. The proposed fix (derive winLoss and the month rollup from Postgres groupBy/date_trunc aggregates scoped to the account, mirroring fetchAccountStats, and keep take:100 only for display lists; or at minimum order the aggregation input by dueDate and raise/remove the cap) is sound.

confirmed.title: Org-dashboard cockpit computes a single account's win/loss + revenue from a 100-row WHOLE-ORG opportunity sample
confirmed.evidence: buildDashboardSnapshot loads opportunities with `where: { orgId, deletedAt: null } ... take: 100` (service.ts:107-108) — 100 rows across the ENTIRE org, ordered updatedAt desc — then passes that array to buildCockpit (service.ts:314-324), which filters to the selected company in JS (cockpit.ts:471-474) and computes winLoss + revenueEvolution from whatever survived. For any org with more than ~100 active opportunities, the selected account will receive only the subset of its deals that happen to be among the org's 100 most-recently-touched — frequently zero or a handful. Result: the dashboard's account cockpit shows win-rate 0% and an empty revenue chart for accounts that actually have rich pipeline, purely as an artifact of the org-wide cap. This is the default dashboard view, so it is the first number a manager sees.
confirmed.fix: The org-dashboard cockpit must not derive per-account win/loss + revenue from an org-wide take:100 sample. Either compute those metrics for the selected company via a company-scoped aggregate query (same fix as buildCompanyCockpit), or have buildDashboardSnapshot reuse buildCompanyCockpit's account-scoped path for the cockpit slice rather than the shared 100-row org list.

confirmed.title: Opportunity lacks the (orgId, companyId) composite index that every other tenant table has — undercuts the new account-aggregation paths
confirmed.evidence: Opportunity declares only `@@index([companyId])` (schema.prisma:450) — a bare single-column index — while Contact (545), Note (1143), FileAttachment (1177), AccountSolution, AccountProduct, BidDocument (1429), ServiceCase (2206) etc. all carry `@@index([orgId, companyId])`. The opportunity table is the outlier. The new high-traffic aggregation paths all filter on `{ orgId, companyId: { in: companyIds }, deletedAt: null }`: accounts.helpers.ts:38 (fetchAccountStats — FOUR opportunity.groupBy calls for the Top-10/curated cockpit), accounts.ts:96 (key-accounts list), and the raw-SQL leaderboard JOIN `o.company_id = c.id AND o.org_id = $orgId AND o.deleted_at IS NULL` (accounts.ts:266-269). With only (companyId), Postgres uses the less-selective single-column index and post-filters orgId/deletedAt; the matching Contact.groupBy on the identical predicate IS backed by (orgId, companyId). As opportunity volume grows this is the table that scales worst and is hit most by the new code.
confirmed.fix: Add `@@index([orgId, companyId], map: "opps_org_company_idx")` to the Opportunity model and ship an additive migration `CREATE INDEX "opps_org_company_idx" ON "opportunities"("org_id", "company_id");`. Optionally include deletedAt as a partial-index predicate (`WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`) to match the always-applied soft-delete filter.

The key-accounts list is the lone JS-reduce holdout.
confirmed.fix: Replace the take:1000 findMany+reduce with the existing fetchAccountStats(orgId, companyIds) helper (it returns exact totals via groupBy and is already imported into this file at accounts.ts:13), or an inline opportunity.groupBy by companyId. This removes the silent cap and unifies the three account-list code paths on one aggregation.

confirmed.title: valueMicros sums reduced in JS via Number() lose integer precision past 2^53 for large enterprise accounts
confirmed.evidence: Money is stored as BigInt micros (×1e6 per the CLAUDE.md convention). The cockpit reduces won/lost value with `toMicros` returning `Number(bigint)` and accumulates with `+` (cockpit.ts:564-567, 587); accounts.ts:113 does `Number(o.valueMicros) / 1_000_000`. JS Number is IEEE-754 with an exact-integer ceiling of 2^53 ≈ 9.007e15. €1B = 1e15 micros, so a cockpit summing ~9 deals at €1B, or ~100 deals averaging €100M (well within the take:100 window), exceeds 2^53 and silently loses least-significant digits in the displayed/total figure. The groupBy and raw-SQL paths are safer because Postgres computes the SUM exactly first (raw SQL casts to float8, which is range-safe though precision-lossy at the same magnitude); the in-JS accumulate has no such protection.
confirmed.fix: Accumulate micros as BigInt (sum bigints, convert to Number/format only at the edge after dividing), or do all valueMicros aggregation in Postgres (groupBy _sum / raw SUM) which this codebase already does elsewhere. The cockpit's toMicros+reduce is the one place that accumulates in float.

verdict.reason:
MECHANISM CONFIRMED by the cited code. `Opportunity.valueMicros` is `BigInt` (packages/db/prisma/schema.prisma:408). The cockpit converts via `toMicros = (v) => Number(v)` and accumulates won/lost with float `+` (apps/api/src/services/crm/dashboard.cockpit.ts:564-567, 587). accounts.ts:113 does `Number(o.valueMicros) / 1_000_000` then float-sums per company. The `take` windows admit totals above 2^53 micros (€9.007B): the cockpit fetch is `take: 100` with NO `_sum` aggregation (dashboard.service.ts:78-108), accounts.ts is `take: 1000`. So the sum genuinely enters the float64 non-exact-integer range, and this is indeed the one in-JS float-accumulation site versus the safer groupBy/_sum and raw-SQL SUM paths used elsewhere — the claim located it correctly.

BUT THE SEVERITY IS OVERSTATED. The claim implies the displayed/total figure silently loses meaningful digits. Quantitatively it does not at any realistic scale: (1) Money is stored in micros but real deals are granular to the cent = 1e4 micros, so cent-multiple values stay EXACTLY representable in float64 up to 2^67 micros ≈ €147 TRILLION (verified). No enterprise account total approaches that. (2) Tested 100 realistic non-round €135M deals summing to €13.5B (well past 2^53 micros): delta = exactly 0. (3) Even adversarial SUB-cent odd micros, 100 deals at €13.5B total, lost only 16 micros = €0.000016 across the whole sum. (4) Worst single Number(bigint) loss for a €9.5B deal = 1 micro = €0.000001. The displayed value is formatted from micros (÷1e6), so any error below one cent (1e4 micros) is invisible — and that threshold isn't reached until ~€147T. 

So the finding is a legitimate code-hygiene/correctness-purity observation (BigInt micros should be accumulated as BigInt or summed in Postgres, and the proposed fix is sound and matches patterns the codebase already uses), but its practical impact is sub-cent and economically/visually null at every realistic enterprise magnitude. Real as a pattern, but below "minor" — trivial/informational, not a user-facing correctness defect.

confirmed.title: sector-view totalAccounts and dataQualityWarning are computed over only the 1000 newest companies, not the org
confirmed.evidence: The sector rollup loads companies with `take: 1000, orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }` (sector-view.ts:47-48) and then reports `totalAccounts: rows.length` (51,97) and computes `dataQualityWarning = classified.length / totalAccounts < 0.6` (99-100) over that capped set. For an org with >1000 companies, totalAccounts caps at 1000 and the classification ratio is measured only against the 1000 most-recently-created companies — so the response field named totalAccounts is misleading and the data-quality gate can flip based on recency, not the real corpus. The query itself is index-backed (companies_org_created_idx on (orgId, createdAt DESC)), so this is correctness/labelling, not a missing index. The inline comment frames the cap as a deliberate 'strategic overview', but the field name implies a full count.
confirmed.fix: Either rename the field to reflect the sample (e.g. sampledAccounts) and document the 1000-cap in the response, or compute totalAccounts and the classified-ratio with a cheap company.count()/groupBy over the full org (indexed) and keep the take:1000 only for the per-sector country rollup detail.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed by the cited code. apps/api/src/routes/sector-view.ts:42-49 issues a single prisma.company.findMany with take:1000 orderBy createdAt desc and no other count/groupBy exists anywhere for this route. Line 51 sets totalAccounts = rows.length (capped at 1000), and lines 99-100 compute dataQualityWarning = totalAccounts===0 || classified.length/totalAccounts < 0.6 over that same capped sample. So for an org with >1000 companies, the response field named totalAccounts caps at 1000 and the data-quality gate is measured only against the 1000 most-recently-created companies — a real labelling/correctness issue and a recency-dependent quality flip, exactly as claimed.

The 1000 cap is a genuine hard ceiling, not arbitrary: prisma-middleware.ts:51-57 flags any findMany with take>1000 (or missing take) as unbounded, and query-guard.ts:60-66 turns that into an HTTP 400 in dev/test (warn in prod). This is a CRM whose orgs in the demo context typically hold <1000 companies, where the field is exactly correct; the defect only manifests above 1000 companies/org as a misleading label and a recency-sensitive quality gate. Correctness/labelling severity = minor is appropriate.

confirmed.title: Account-cockpit read endpoints are not RBAC-gated (any authenticated org member reads revenue / win-loss / key-account notes)
confirmed.evidence: GET /accounts/key (line 40), GET /accounts/top (line 146) and GET /accounts/industries (line 457) have no `preHandler`. The global auth hook (apps/api/src/plugins/auth.ts:368) only sets req.auth; it does NOT enforce permissions — authorization is per-route via requirePermission (apps/api/src/plugins/rbac.ts:47). Queries ARE org-scoped (where:{orgId}) so this is an in-tenant RBAC bypass, not cross-tenant leakage. Mitigating context: legacy reads (reports.ts, opportunities.ts list, leads) follow the same ungated convention, so this is consistent with the existing codebase posture rather than a new regression.
confirmed.fix: Add `preHandler: server.requirePermission('accounts:read')` to the three GET /accounts/* routes, matching the gate already used on infosearch.ts:38. Decide org-wide whether sensitive reads should be permission-gated and apply consistently.

verdict.reason:
VERIFIED REAL. Every cited fact checks out against the code:

1. The three cockpit reads in apps/api/src/routes/accounts.ts have NO preHandler: GET /accounts/key (line 40), GET /accounts/top (line 146), GET /accounts/industries (line 457). Each only does `const { orgId } = req.auth` — no requirePermission gate. By contrast the write routes in the SAME file ARE gated: PUT /accounts/top-list (line 316, accounts:write) and PATCH /companies/:id/tier (line 371, accounts:write).

It checks UserRole→Role→permissions for the exact key and throws 403 on miss, with NO admin/claim fallback (deliberately removed per ADR-0001). Rationale: (a) it is an in-tenant authorization gap among authenticated, same-org members — not a data leak to outsiders or across tenants; (b) it is consistent with the codebase's pervasive ungated-read posture (reports.ts, opportunities.ts list), so it is a posture-consistency issue rather than a novel regression; (c) the most sensitive aggregate data (pipeline/won revenue) is ALREADY reachable ungated through /reports/pipeline, so the marginal new exposure is per-account granularity plus the free-text keyAccountNotes field — real but narrow; (d) realistic exploitation requires an admin to have deliberately created a custom role that grants other access but withholds accounts:read, while the 6 seeded system roles (including Read-Only) all include accounts:read, so the default deployment is not exposed.
